claim: PGAM1 was the most differentially expressed glycolytic gene in human iTregs compared to Th0 cells
source: After library normalization, we examined genes included in the 'Glycolysis and Gluconeogenesis' gene ontology (GO) term and found that PGAM1 was the most differentially expressed glycolytic gene, with upregulation in in vitro-induced Tregs (iTregs) compared to conventional Th0 cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1A comparing human naïve CD4 cells cultured under Th0 or Treg polarizing conditions

claim: PGAM1 is upregulated in ex vivo-derived Tregs compared to total CD4 cells
source: To determine whether PGAM expression is similarly upregulated in ex vivo-derived Tregs, we examined a single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) dataset of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy human controls (Schafflick et al., 2020) and compared glycolytic gene expression between Tregs and total CD4 cells. After removing glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) for scaling purposes, we found that PGAM1 was similarly upregulated in Tregs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data analysis from healthy human PBMCs shown in Figure 1B

claim: PGAM1 and PGAM2 protein levels are significantly upregulated in Tregs compared to total CD4 cells
source: A proteomics dataset from human healthy donor PBMCs Procaccini et al., 2016 demonstrated significantly upregulated protein levels of PGAM1 and PGAM2 in Tregs compared to total CD4 cells (Figure 1C), confirming findings from the mRNA level.
evidence: Supported by proteomics data from human healthy donor PBMCs shown in Figure 1C

claim: Treatment with EGCG significantly reduced Treg differentiation
source: We cultured naïve murine CD4 cells under Treg polarizing conditions with either vehicle (solvent alone) or EGCG and assessed Treg differentiation by quantifying the percentage of CD25+FOXP3+ cells by flow cytometry after 96 hr. Treatment with EGCG significantly reduced Treg differentiation (Figure 1D) without affecting proliferation or cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced CD25+FOXP3+ cells with EGCG treatment shown in Figure 1D

claim: ASOs targeting Pgam reduced PGAM1 protein levels and significantly reduced Treg differentiation
source: Compared to scrambled control ASOs, we found that ASOs targeting Pgam reduced PGAM1 protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and significantly reduced Treg differentiation assessed by flow cytometry (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced PGAM1 protein and Treg differentiation with Pgam ASOs shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Pgam ASOs did not affect cell survival and led to a minor increase in cell proliferation
source: We found that Pgam ASOs did not affect cell survival and led to a minor increase in cell proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data on cell viability and proliferation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Pgam ASOs led to major transcriptional changes in CD4 T cells cultured under Treg polarizing conditions
source: PCA analysis showed that Pgam ASOs led to major transcriptional changes (Figure 1F), with major effects on MYC targets and mTORC1 signaling (Figure 1G), among other changes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing PCA separation and GSEA results shown in Figures 1F and 1G

claim: Cells treated with Pgam ASOs had significantly higher expression of pro-inflammatory genes such as Il17, Il22, and Il9, while significantly lower expression of genes involved in Treg differentiation such as Foxp3 and Izkf3
source: We then performed differential expression analysis on a subset of genes important in the Treg-Th17 axis and found that cells treated with Pgam ASOs had significantly higher expression of pro-inflammatory genes such as Il17, Il22, and Il9, while significantly lower expression of genes involved in Treg differentiation such as Foxp3 and Izkf3 (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1H

claim: Pgam ASO-treated Tregs were less effective at suppressing effector T cell proliferation
source: Compared to treatment with scrambled ASOs, Pgam ASO-treated Tregs were less effective at suppressing effector T (Teff) cell proliferation, indicating diminished suppressive function (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by Treg suppression assay data shown in Figure 1I

claim: PGAM1 was significantly overexpressed in the highly suppressive OX40hiGITRhi TIL-Treg cluster compared to 9 other TIL-Treg subsets
source: Strikingly, PGAM1 was significantly overexpressed in the highly suppressive OX40hiGITRhi cluster compared to the 9 other TIL-Treg subsets (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published scRNA-seq data from tumor-infiltrating Tregs shown in Figure 1J

claim: PGAM1 expression was selectively increased in the highly suppressive OX40hiGITRhi TIL-Treg cluster relative to proximal, rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes
source: Moreover, PGAM1 expression was selectively increased in this subset relative to proximal, rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes, suggesting a unique association between PGAM expression and Treg suppressive activity.
evidence: Supported by analysis of published scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1J

claim: Inhibition of GAPDH with koningic acid increased Treg differentiation
source: Indeed, whereas inhibition or knockdown of PGAM led to decreased Treg differentiation, our own prior work found that similar inhibition of GAPDH, which catalyzes a reaction only two steps upstream from PGAM in glycolysis, had the opposite effect (Kornberg et al., 2018) – a finding we replicated here with the GAPDH inhibitor koningic acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citation to prior work

claim: The ratio of PGAM1 to GAPDH mRNA levels increased in human iTregs vs. Th0 cells
source: Consistent with this observation, the ratio of PGAM1 to GAPDH mRNA levels increased in human iTregs vs. Th0 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), and PGAM2 protein levels increased out of proportion to GAPDH (and other glycolytic enzymes) in ex vivo Tregs (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: PGAM2 protein levels increased out of proportion to GAPDH in ex vivo Tregs
source: Consistent with this observation, the ratio of PGAM1 to GAPDH mRNA levels increased in human iTregs vs. Th0 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), and PGAM2 protein levels increased out of proportion to GAPDH (and other glycolytic enzymes) in ex vivo Tregs (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 1C

claim: PGAM1/GAPDH protein copy number ratio is increased in murine iTregs versus Th17 cells
source: Similarly, a review of published data from the ImmPres immunological proteome resource (http://immpres.co.uk/; Brenes et al., 2023) shows increased PGAM1/GAPDH protein copy number ratio in murine iTregs versus Th17 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), further implicating a specific role for PGAM in the Treg-Th17 axis.
evidence: Supported by analysis of published proteomics data from ImmPres resource shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: PGAM inhibition with EGCG increased intracellular levels of serine in Tregs
source: To test this hypothesis, we first cultured naïve murine CD4 cells under Treg polarizing conditions with either vehicle or the PGAM inhibitor EGCG and measured intracellular serine levels from unsorted cells by mass spectrometry. As anticipated, PGAM inhibition with EGCG increased intracellular levels of serine in Tregs (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS data showing increased serine levels with EGCG treatment shown in Figure 2B

claim: 13C-labeling of serine was significantly higher in Th17 cells compared to Tregs
source: We differentiated naïve murine CD4 cells into either Tregs or Th17 cells for 72 hr. After 6 hr glucose starvation, the cells were incubated with U13C-glucose for an additional 6 hr. Using mass spectrometry, we found that 13C-labeling of serine was significantly higher in Th17 cells compared to Tregs (Figure 2C), indicating that flux through de novo serine synthesis is physiologically downregulated in Tregs compared to Th17 cells.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Flux through de novo serine synthesis is physiologically downregulated in Tregs compared to Th17 cells
source: Using mass spectrometry, we found that 13C-labeling of serine was significantly higher in Th17 cells compared to Tregs (Figure 2C), indicating that flux through de novo serine synthesis is physiologically downregulated in Tregs compared to Th17 cells.
evidence: Inferred from isotope tracing data showing higher 13C-serine in Th17 cells shown in Figure 2C

claim: PHGDH inhibition with NCT-503 reversed the inhibitory effect of EGCG on Treg differentiation
source: As before, PGAM inhibition with EGCG inhibited Treg differentiation as assessed by FOXP3 expression, but this was reversed by PHGDH inhibition with NCT-503 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing rescue of Treg differentiation with NCT-503 shown in Figure 2D

claim: 3 PG supplementation decreased FOXP3 expression, which was rescued by PHGDH inhibition with NCT-503
source: To test this, 3 PG was delivered to naïve murine CD4 cells via electroporation, followed by Treg polarization. As expected, 3 PG supplementation decreased FOXP3 expression, which was rescued by PHGDH inhibition with NCT-503 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing decreased FOXP3 with 3PG and rescue with NCT-503 shown in Figure 2E

claim: Genetic knockdown of PHGDH led to augmented Treg differentiation
source: To further validate the role of de novo serine synthesis in Tregs, we used Phgdh-targeted ASOs and found that genetic knockdown of PHGDH led to augmented Treg differentiation as assessed by FOXP3 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased FOXP3 with Phgdh ASOs shown in Figure 2F

claim: The presence of extracellular serine diminished Treg differentiation
source: We cultured naïve murine CD4 cells under Treg polarizing conditions in either serine/glycine-free media or serine/glycine-free media supplemented with 4 mM serine. Deprivation of both serine and glycine is required to evaluate the role of extracellular serine, as glycine can be converted to serine via the enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) (He et al., 2023). The presence of extracellular serine diminished Treg differentiation (Figure 2G), indicating that both synthesized and exogenous serine impact Treg generation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing decreased Treg differentiation with serine supplementation shown in Figure 2G

claim: Both synthesized and exogenous serine impact Treg generation
source: The presence of extracellular serine diminished Treg differentiation (Figure 2G), indicating that both synthesized and exogenous serine impact Treg generation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings that both PHGDH inhibition and extracellular serine affect Treg differentiation

claim: Mice fed a serine/glycine-free diet had significantly higher proportions of Tregs in peripheral blood
source: After 8 weeks, we measured Treg abundance in peripheral blood by flow cytometry. Mice fed a serine/glycine-free diet had significantly higher proportions of Tregs in peripheral blood (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from peripheral blood of mice on serine/glycine-free diet shown in Figure 3A

claim: A serine/glycine-free diet significantly attenuated disease severity in the MOG35-55 EAE model
source: Mice were transitioned to a serine/glycine-free or isocaloric control diet beginning one week prior to immunization with MOG35-55, and disease severity was monitored by a blinded scorer. A serine/glycine-free diet significantly attenuated disease severity, delaying the onset of neurologic deficits and reducing peak clinical scores (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by clinical scoring data from EAE model shown in Figures 3B-D

claim: Serine synthesis was downregulated in human iTregs compared to Th0 cells
source: We applied SCFEA to human Th0 and iTreg cells differentiated from naïve CD4 cells in vitro (Ullah et al., 2018) and found that serine synthesis was downregulated in iTregs (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by SCFEA analysis of published RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The predicted rate of serine synthesis was significantly higher in Tregs from MS patients compared to controls
source: Using scRNA-seq data derived from Tregs isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with treatment-naïve relapsing MS and controls (Schafflick et al., 2020), we found the predicted rate of serine synthesis was significantly higher in Tregs from MS patients (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by SCFEA analysis of published scRNA-seq data from MS patients shown in Figure 3F

claim: Prostate tumor-infiltrating Tregs had significantly lower predicted serine synthesis than Tregs from healthy prostate
source: We examined scRNA-seq data from Tregs derived from healthy prostate and prostate cancer (Tuong et al., 2021) from the IMMUcan database (Camps et al., 2023) and found that prostate tumor-infiltrating Tregs had significantly lower predicted serine synthesis than Tregs from healthy prostate (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by SCFEA analysis of published scRNA-seq data from prostate cancer shown in Figure 3G

claim: Serine synthesis within Tregs is higher in autoimmunity and lower in the tumor microenvironment, thereby negatively correlating with expected Treg suppressive function in human disease
source: Consistent with our earlier findings that serine synthesis inhibits Treg function, these analyses suggest that serine synthesis within Tregs is higher in autoimmunity and lower in the tumor microenvironment, thereby negatively correlating with expected Treg suppressive function in human disease.
evidence: Inferred from SCFEA analyses showing higher serine synthesis in MS Tregs and lower in tumor Tregs

claim: Inhibiting SHMT1/2 increased Treg polarization
source: To determine whether the effects of serine on Treg differentiation depend on contributions to one-carbon metabolism, we cultured naïve murine CD4 cells under Treg polarizing conditions with either vehicle or the SHMT1/2 inhibitor SHIN1 (Makino et al., 2022; Ducker et al., 2017). Inhibiting SHMT1/2 increased Treg polarization (Figure 4B) and mitigated the inhibitory effect of extracellular serine on Tregs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased Treg polarization with SHIN1 shown in Figure 4B

claim: SHMT1/2 inhibition mitigated the inhibitory effect of extracellular serine on Tregs
source: Inhibiting SHMT1/2 increased Treg polarization (Figure 4B) and mitigated the inhibitory effect of extracellular serine on Tregs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing rescue of Treg polarization with SHIN1 in presence of serine shown in Figure 4C

claim: Excess extracellular serine (4 mM) was highly potent in inhibiting Treg polarization in the absence of methionine
source: To further the idea that serine inhibits Treg polarization by contributing to one-carbon metabolism, we cultured naïve murine CD4 cells under Treg polarizing conditions in methionine-free media supplemented with either methionine or excess serine. Although methionine supplementation had little effect in the presence of physiologic extracellular serine (0.4 mM), excess extracellular serine (4 mM) was highly potent in inhibiting Treg polarization in the absence of methionine (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing strong inhibition of Treg polarization with 4 mM serine in methionine-free media shown in Figure 4D

claim: Serine directly contributed to cytosine methylation in Tregs
source: We, therefore, asked whether serine entry into one-carbon metabolism contributes to DNA methylation in Tregs, so we conducted a carbon tracing experiment in which Tregs were cultured in media containing uniformly 13-carbon-labeled serine (U13C-serine) for 12 hr before DNA was isolated from the unsorted cells and analyzed by mass spectrometry. We found that serine directly contributed to cytosine methylation, as measured by carbon labeling of methylcytosine (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS isotope tracing data showing 13C-labeled methylcytosine from 13C-serine shown in Figure 4E

claim: The presence of extracellular serine increased TSDR methylation
source: In a first set of experiments, naïve murine CD4 cells were cultured under Treg polarizing conditions in either serine/glycine-free media or media containing serine. The presence of extracellular serine increased TSDR methylation (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by pyrosequencing data showing increased TSDR methylation with serine shown in Figure 4F

claim: Genetic knockdown of PGAM using ASOs increased TSDR methylation
source: Genetic knockdown of PGAM using ASOs similarly increased TSDR methylation (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by pyrosequencing data showing increased TSDR methylation with Pgam ASOs shown in Figure 4G

claim: Both extracellular serine and PGAM-regulated serine synthesis increase the methylation, and therefore silencing, of Treg-associated genes
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that both extracellular serine and PGAM-regulated serine synthesis increase the methylation, and therefore silencing, of Treg-associated genes.
evidence: Inferred from pyrosequencing data showing increased TSDR methylation with both serine and PGAM knockdown

claim: Methylation of Ikzf2 (Helios) was significantly increased with the addition of extracellular serine, but this was reversed by blocking serine entry into one-carbon metabolism with the SHMT inhibitor SHIN1
source: Methylation of Ikzf2 (Helios) was significantly increased with the addition of extracellular serine, but this was reversed by blocking serine entry into one-carbon metabolism with the SHMT inhibitor SHIN1.
evidence: Supported by next generation sequencing methylation data shown in Figure 4H

claim: One CpG site in the 5' upstream region of the Foxp3 gene showed significantly higher methylation in the presence of serine, and this effect was reversed by SHIN1
source: In the 5' upstream region of the Foxp3 gene, one CpG site showed significantly higher methylation in the presence of serine, and this effect was reversed by SHIN1.
evidence: Supported by next generation sequencing methylation data shown in Figure 4H

claim: 3DZA increased Treg differentiation without affecting cell viability
source: In naïve murine CD4 cells cultured under Treg polarizing conditions, 3DZA increased Treg differentiation (Figure 4I) without affecting cell viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased Treg differentiation with 3DZA shown in Figure 4I and viability data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Treatment with 3DZA augmented suppressive function in cultured murine Tregs
source: Treatment with 3DZA similarly augmented suppressive function in cultured murine Tregs (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by Treg suppression assay data shown in Figure 4J

claim: Mice injected with Tregs polarized in the presence of 3DZA had less severe disease as measured by weight loss and colonic damage in the RAG colitis model
source: Conventional murine CD4 cells were activated ex vivo and injected into RAG-/- mice to induce colitis, along with simultaneous injection of Tregs that had been treated during differentiation with either vehicle or 3DZA. Mice injected with Tregs polarized in the presence of 3DZA had less severe disease as measured by weight loss and colonic damage (Figure 4K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating greater Treg suppressive function.
evidence: Supported by weight loss data and colonic damage images from RAG colitis model shown in Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: One-carbon metabolism and methylation impair Treg differentiation and suppressive function both in vitro and in vivo
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate that one-carbon metabolism and methylation impair Treg differentiation and suppressive function both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from combined findings showing that inhibiting one-carbon metabolism and methylation increases Treg function in vitro and in vivo

claim: PGAM plays a key physiologic role in Treg differentiation and suppressive function through regulation of serine synthesis
source: In this study, we found that PGAM plays a key physiologic role in Treg differentiation and suppressive function through regulation of serine synthesis, which intersects with glycolysis immediately upstream of PGAM through the shared substrate 3 PG.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings showing PGAM inhibition reduces Treg function and increases serine synthesis

claim: PGAM expression is enriched in highly suppressive Treg phenotypes
source: Analysis of published datasets revealed that PGAM expression is specifically increased within human Tregs at both transcriptional and protein levels, and further that PGAM expression is enriched in highly suppressive Treg phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by analysis of multiple published datasets showing PGAM upregulation in Tregs and highly suppressive TIL-Treg subsets

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition or genetic knockdown of PGAM reduced Treg polarization and suppressive function while promoting a pro-inflammatory gene signature
source: Pharmacologic inhibition or genetic knockdown of PGAM reduced Treg polarization and suppressive function while promoting a pro-inflammatory gene signature.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry, RNA-seq, and functional assay data showing reduced Treg function and increased pro-inflammatory markers with PGAM inhibition

claim: The effects of PGAM inhibition were replicated by exogenous supplementation of 3 PG and reversed by inhibition of serine synthesis
source: These effects were replicated by exogenous supplementation of 3 PG and reversed by inhibition of serine synthesis.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing that 3PG supplementation reduces Treg differentiation and PHGDH inhibition rescues the effect of PGAM inhibition

claim: Serine inhibited Treg polarization by increasing flux through one-carbon metabolism with downstream effects on DNA methylation of Treg-related genes
source: Mechanistically, serine inhibited Treg polarization by increasing flux through one-carbon metabolism with downstream effects on DNA methylation of Treg-related genes.
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing, methylation sequencing, and functional assay data showing serine contributes to methylation and inhibits Treg function

claim: Interfering with serine availability or methylation attenuated disease in in vivo models of autoimmunity
source: Interfering with serine availability or methylation attenuated disease in in vivo models of autoimmunity.
evidence: Supported by EAE and RAG colitis model data showing reduced disease severity with serine/glycine-free diet and methylation inhibition

claim: Glycolytic regulation of immunity is more complex than previously appreciated, supporting a more granular view in which glycolytic enzymes can serve as independent regulatory nodes for the fine-tuning of immune responses
source: These findings suggest that glycolytic regulation of immunity is more complex than previously appreciated, supporting a more granular view in which glycolytic enzymes can serve as independent regulatory nodes for the fine-tuning of immune responses.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting effects of PGAM and GAPDH inhibition on Treg differentiation

claim: Differential effects of glycolytic enzymes might be mediated by fine control of the metabolites whose concentrations they regulate, such as 3 PG in the case of PGAM
source: Our data suggest that these differential effects of glycolytic enzymes might be mediated by fine control of the metabolites whose concentrations they regulate, such as 3 PG in the case of PGAM.
evidence: Inferred from data showing that 3PG supplementation replicates the effects of PGAM inhibition

claim: Manipulation of PGAM and downstream serine metabolism and DNA methylation is a potential strategy for improving the anti-cancer fitness of CAR-T cells ex vivo prior to infusion
source: Differentiation of CAR-T cells into a Treg-like state correlates with failure of CAR-T therapy in B cell lymphoma (Good et al., 2022), such that manipulation of PGAM and downstream serine metabolism and DNA methylation is a potential strategy for improving the anti-cancer fitness of CAR-T cells ex vivo prior to infusion.
evidence: Speculative application based on findings that PGAM inhibition reduces Treg differentiation, combined with citation showing Treg-like state correlates with CAR-T failure

claim: Complete knockout of PGAM1 in T cells impaired differentiation and effector functions of pro-inflammatory T cell subsets with only a mild impact on Treg generation
source: Of note, a prior study reported that complete knockout of PGAM1 in T cells impaired differentiation and effector functions of pro-inflammatory T cell subsets with only a mild impact on Treg generation (Toriyama et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from prior published study

claim: Complete knockout of a glycolytic enzyme would be expected to abrogate glycolytic flux entirely, with wide-ranging effects likely to mask the impact of physiologic or therapeutic modulation of enzyme function
source: However, complete knockout of a glycolytic enzyme would be expected to abrogate glycolytic flux entirely, with wide-ranging effects (including decreased energy production) likely to mask the impact of physiologic or therapeutic modulation of enzyme function.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of glycolysis and reasoning about the effects of complete enzyme knockout

claim: Partial knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition of PGAM1 substantially reduced Treg differentiation while supporting pro-inflammatory activation
source: As we showed here, partial knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition of PGAM1, which decreases but does not fully abrogate enzymatic activity, substantially reduced Treg differentiation while supporting pro-inflammatory activation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RNA-seq data showing reduced Treg differentiation and increased pro-inflammatory markers with PGAM inhibition

claim: PGAM supports tumor proliferation by controlling flux through the de novo serine synthesis pathway
source: Additionally, other groups studying glycolysis in cancer used partial knockdowns to show that PGAM supports tumor proliferation by controlling flux through the de novo serine synthesis pathway (Itoyama et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from prior published study on PGAM in cancer

claim: One-carbon metabolism contributes to many cellular processes, including purine synthesis, amino acid metabolism, and phospholipid synthesis
source: However, one-carbon metabolism contributes to many cellular processes, including purine synthesis, amino acid metabolism, and phospholipid synthesis, among others (Mentch and Locasale, 2016), so it is likely that one-carbon metabolism inhibits Treg differentiation in a variety of ways.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of one-carbon metabolism cited from prior work

claim: Demethylation of the Treg-specific demethylated region (TSDR) in Tregs is a critical step for the generation of stable, bona fide Tregs
source: Demethylation of the Treg-specific demethylated region (TSDR) in Tregs is a critical step for the generation of stable, bona fide Tregs, and methylation in this region is associated with transient or unstable expression of FOXP3 and suppressive activity (Polansky et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from prior work

claim: Methylation in the TSDR is associated with transient or unstable expression of FOXP3 and suppressive activity
source: Demethylation of the Treg-specific demethylated region (TSDR) in Tregs is a critical step for the generation of stable, bona fide Tregs, and methylation in this region is associated with transient or unstable expression of FOXP3 and suppressive activity (Polansky et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from prior work

claim: 3 PG is the starting substrate for the de novo serine synthesis pathway
source: In addition to its role in glycolysis, 3 PG is the starting substrate for the de novo serine synthesis pathway (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011; He et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of serine synthesis pathway cited from prior work

claim: PGAM converts 3-phosphoglycerate (3 PG) to 2-phosphoglycerate (2 PG)
source: PGAM metabolizes the glycolytic intermediate 3 PG into 2 PG (DiMauro et al., 1981; Koo and Oskarsson, 2016).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PGAM enzyme function cited from prior work

claim: Glycine can be converted to serine via the enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT)
source: Deprivation of both serine and glycine is required to evaluate the role of extracellular serine, as glycine can be converted to serine via the enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) (He et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of serine-glycine interconversion cited from prior work

claim: Serine can serve as a one-carbon donor by entering the one-carbon metabolism cycle, which depends on conversion into glycine by the enzyme SHMT1/2
source: Serine can serve as a one-carbon donor by entering the one-carbon metabolism cycle, which depends on conversion into glycine by the enzyme SHMT1/2 (Reina-Campos et al., 2020; Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of one-carbon metabolism cited from prior work and illustrated in Figure 4A

claim: The contribution of serine to one-carbon metabolism is greater in the absence of methionine
source: Because methionine can compensate as a one-carbon donor, other groups have found that the contribution of serine to one-carbon metabolism is greater in the absence of methionine (Maddocks et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior published study

claim: Increased glucose uptake and augmented glycolysis are critical for the differentiation and effector functions of inflammatory T cell subsets, including effector CD8 cells and T-helper (Th) 1 and Th17 CD4 cells
source: Increased glucose uptake and augmented glycolysis are critical for the differentiation and effector functions of inflammatory T cell subsets, including effector CD8 cells and T-helper (Th) 1 and Th17 CD4 cells (Frauwirth et al., 2002; Cham and Gajewski, 2005; Cham et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2013; Macintyre et al., 2014; Gerriets et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple cited studies

claim: Initial engagement of glycolysis supports proliferation and migration of Tregs
source: Prior work has shown that initial engagement of glycolysis supports proliferation and migration of Tregs, whereas downregulation of glycolysis and greater engagement of fatty acid oxidation are required for expression of the Treg-specific transcription factor FOXP3 and Treg suppressive functions (Ho et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020; Lim et al., 2021; Kishore et al., 2017; Michalek et al., 2011; Gerriets et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple cited studies

claim: Downregulation of glycolysis and greater engagement of fatty acid oxidation are required for expression of the Treg-specific transcription factor FOXP3 and Treg suppressive functions
source: Prior work has shown that initial engagement of glycolysis supports proliferation and migration of Tregs, whereas downregulation of glycolysis and greater engagement of fatty acid oxidation are required for expression of the Treg-specific transcription factor FOXP3 and Treg suppressive functions (Ho et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020; Lim et al., 2021; Kishore et al., 2017; Michalek et al., 2011; Gerriets et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple cited studies

claim: Forced engagement of glycolysis was found to decrease FOXP3 expression
source: In this regard, forced engagement of glycolysis was found to decrease FOXP3 expression (Wei et al., 2016) while inhibition of glycolysis favored Treg differentiation and suppressive functions (Shi et al., 2011; Scherlinger et al., 2022; Kornberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from prior published study

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis favored Treg differentiation and suppressive functions
source: In this regard, forced engagement of glycolysis was found to decrease FOXP3 expression (Wei et al., 2016) while inhibition of glycolysis favored Treg differentiation and suppressive functions (Shi et al., 2011; Scherlinger et al., 2022; Kornberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple cited studies

claim: In human Tregs induced following weak stimulation of the T cell receptor (TCR), glycolysis supported Treg suppressive function by regulating DNA-binding activity of the glycolytic enzyme enolase-1 (ENO1)
source: For instance, in human Tregs induced following weak stimulation of the T cell receptor (TCR), glycolysis supported Treg suppressive function by regulating DNA-binding activity of the glycolytic enzyme enolase-1 (ENO1) (De Rosa et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior published study

claim: Individual glycolytic enzymes can serve unique and perhaps disparate functions in Tregs
source: Such findings suggest the possibility of a more nuanced role for glycolysis in Tregs, with individual glycolytic enzymes serving unique and perhaps disparate functions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different glycolytic enzymes have different effects on Treg function

claim: EGCG is a known inhibitor of PGAM
source: To answer this question, we used epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a known inhibitor of PGAM (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from prior published study

claim: Near-complete ASO uptake by cultured CD4 cells occurs after 24 hr
source: Experiments conducted with fluorescently-tagged ASOs demonstrated near-complete ASO uptake by cultured CD4 cells after 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing fluorescent ASO uptake shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The OX40hiGITRhi TIL-Treg cluster had markedly increased suppressive activity and was enriched in patients who were resistant to immune checkpoint blockade
source: Among the 10 distinct subsets of TIL-Tregs identified in this study, one subset, the OX40hiGITRhi cluster [termed 'Activated (1)' by the authors] had markedly increased suppressive activity and was enriched in patients who were resistant to immune checkpoint blockade.
evidence: Cited from published scRNA-seq study of tumor-infiltrating Tregs

claim: Serine can be recycled via one-carbon metabolism
source: Because serine can be recycled via one-carbon metabolism, we observed an increase in one-carbon-labeled (M+1) serine as well as M+3 serine in Th17 cells relative to Treg cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of one-carbon metabolism and observed isotope labeling patterns

claim: SCFEA constructs a global set of metabolic reactions as a factor map and uses multi-layer neural networks to model reaction rates from mRNA levels of metabolic enzymes
source: Using publicly available RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data, we estimated the rate of de novo serine synthesis using single-cell flux estimation analysis (SCFEA) (Alghamdi et al., 2021), which constructs a global set of metabolic reactions as a factor map and uses multi-layer neural networks to model reaction rates from mRNA levels of metabolic enzymes.
evidence: Description of SCFEA method cited from prior published work

claim: DNA methylation represents a key epigenetic mechanism used to silence gene transcription
source: A crucial role of one-carbon metabolism is to provide methyl groups for methylation reactions, and DNA methylation represents a key epigenetic mechanism used to silence gene transcription (Mentch and Locasale, 2016).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of DNA methylation cited from prior work

claim: SAH hydrolase degrades SAH and prevents recycling of the methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)
source: SAH hydrolase degrades SAH and prevents recycling of the methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) (Jeong et al., 1999).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SAH hydrolase function cited from prior work

claim: Manipulation of glycolysis and other metabolic pathways has a therapeutic window for systemic administration despite the ubiquity of these pathways in cell biology
source: Substantial prior work has shown that manipulation of glycolysis and other metabolic pathways has a therapeutic window for systemic administration despite the ubiquity of these pathways in cell biology (Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from prior published work

claim: Differentiation of CAR-T cells into a Treg-like state correlates with failure of CAR-T therapy in B cell lymphoma
